questions.q: Why does Mara base the Hartwell checklist on the CIS Benchmarks instead of writing her own list of settings from scratch?
options: Because CIS Benchmarks are required by Microsoft Sentinel
Because they're a consensus-built, vendor-independent standard that gives a checkable, defensible answer instead of a personal judgment call
Because CIS Benchmarks only cover Windows Server
Because writing a custom checklist is against Hartwell policy
questions.explain: A published, vendor-independent standard turns "hardened" into something concrete and checkable — "we applied CIS Level 1" is a defensible claim in a way "we tightened things up" is not.

questions.q: Why does Mara scope to CIS Level 1 rather than Level 2 for this project?
options: Level 2 doesn't exist for Linux
Level 1 is basic hardening with minimal business impact, which fits a first project on production billing and outage systems; Level 2's stricter settings risk breaking things without buy-in yet
Level 1 is required by law for utilities
Level 2 only applies to cloud platforms
questions.explain: Level 2 is a reasonable future step, but breaking a production integration during a first security project would cost more trust than it buys — Level 1 matches the stakes of this engagement.

questions.q: What does "scoping the checklist to four real servers" mean in practice?
options: Applying every CIS Level 1 and Level 2 setting, for every platform, everywhere at once
Picking only the specific checks that actually apply to HRU-FILE01, HRU-APP01, hru-web01, and hru-db01, and leaving the rest off deliberately
Skipping the checklist entirely and relying on Windows Defender alone
Applying the Linux checklist to the Windows servers for consistency
questions.explain: A full CIS Benchmark has hundreds of settings, most irrelevant to these specific machines — scoping means choosing the subset that actually matters for exactly these four servers.

questions.q: Which of these is explicitly left OFF this project's checklist, and stated as such?
options: SSH hardening on the Linux servers
Account lockout policy on the Windows servers
CIS Level 2 settings and a platform-wide rollout beyond the four named servers
Windows Firewall rules on the Domain profile
questions.explain: Level 2 settings and a wider rollout are real follow-on work, but they're explicitly out of scope for this first, proven-out pass on four representative servers.

questions.q: Why is a scoped, dozen-item checklist against four named servers a stronger deliverable than a 200-item checklist covering everything Hartwell owns?
options: Because shorter documents are always better regardless of content
Because a smaller, verified checklist actually gets implemented correctly and Dale can tell exactly what it covers and trust it, instead of most of it going unverified under time pressure
Because CIS only publishes short checklists
Because Dale specifically asked for fewer than twelve items
questions.explain: A checklist that's actually verified end to end, against real named servers, is more trustworthy than a sprawling one that looks thorough on paper but mostly doesn't get checked.
